Physical chiral components obey $\psi_{\mathrm{raw}}=\sqrt2\psi$ and $F_{\mathrm{raw}}=2F$. All physical action and coupling formulas below use these brackets and physical component names; adding Hermitian conjugation applies only to the F action and occurs once.

Use oriented and time-oriented Minkowski spacetime $M=\mathbb R^{1,3}$ with coordinates $x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3$, metric $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and natural units $\hbar=c=1$. Let $n\geq1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb C^n$ be an open set containing $0$, let $K:U\to\mathbb R$ be smooth, and require the Hermitian matrix $g_{i\bar j}(z,\bar z)=\partial_i\partial_{\bar j}K(z,\bar z)$ to be positive definite at every point of $U$. Let $W:U\to\mathbb C$ be smooth and holomorphic, where holomorphic means $\partial_{\bar i}W=0$ for every $i$, using the Wirtinger derivatives of the Kähler coordinate-patch definition; write $W_i=\partial_iW$. These data specify the Kähler coordinate patch and holomorphic superpotential of the model.

For these classical fields, take a finite-dimensional exterior algebra $\mathcal G$ over $\mathbb C$ on ordered odd generators $\zeta_1,\ldots,\zeta_m$ for $m\geq0$, with componentwise complex addition and multiplication modulo $\zeta_a^2=0$ and $\zeta_a\zeta_b=-\zeta_b\zeta_a$. Give it the conjugate-linear operation $(c\zeta_{i_1}\cdots\zeta_{i_r})^*=\bar c\zeta_{i_r}\cdots\zeta_{i_1}$, so $\zeta_a^*=\zeta_a$, $(uv)^*=v^*u^*$ and $(u^*)^*=u$. Reversing twice proves involutivity, and reversing the defining relations preserves them; thus this is a well-defined parity-preserving anti-automorphism. Write $\mathcal G_{\bar0},\mathcal G_{\bar1}$ for its even and odd subspaces, and use its degree-zero projection $b:\mathcal G\to\mathbb C$. Form the graded tensor product $\mathcal B=\mathcal G\otimes_{\mathbb C}\Lambda_4$ with the superspace Grassmann algebra, and let $\mathfrak J$ be the ideal of elements with zero total degree-zero part. Then $\mathfrak J^{m+5}=0$. For an even superfield $\Phi^i$, its body is its image under the augmentation $\mathcal B\to\mathbb C$ that applies $b$ and sends all superspace generators to zero; denote that ordinary scalar component by $\phi^i(x)$. Write $\bar\Phi^{\bar i}=(\Phi^i)^*$, $\nu^i=\Phi^i-\phi^i$, and $\bar\nu^{\bar i}=\bar\Phi^{\bar i}-\bar\phi^{\bar i}$; these differences lie in $\mathfrak J$. Define the smooth function's value on the full superfields by the finite nilpotent Taylor convention

$$K(\bar\Phi,\Phi):=\sum_{\substack{\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb N^n\\|\alpha|+|\beta|\leq m+4}}\frac{(\partial_z^\alpha\partial_{\bar z}^\beta K)(\phi,\bar\phi)}{\alpha!\,\beta!}(\nu)^\alpha(\bar\nu)^\beta,$$

where $\alpha!=\prod_i\alpha_i!$, $\beta!=\prod_i\beta_i!$, $\nu^\alpha=\prod_i(\nu^i)^{\alpha_i}$, $(\bar\nu)^\beta=\prod_i(\bar\nu^{\bar i})^{\beta_i}$, $\partial_z^\alpha=\prod_i\partial_i^{\alpha_i}$, $\partial_{\bar z}^\beta=\prod_i\partial_{\bar i}^{\beta_i}$, and the coefficient derivatives are evaluated at $(\phi(x),\bar\phi(x))$. Define the holomorphic superfield evaluation and its derivatives by the finite Taylor rule at the scalar body,

$$W(\Phi)(x,\theta,\bar\theta):=\sum_{|\alpha|\leq m+4}\frac{(\partial_z^\alpha W)(\phi(x))}{\alpha!}(\nu)^\alpha,\qquad W_i(\Phi):=\sum_{|\alpha|\leq m+4}\frac{(\partial_z^\alpha\partial_iW)(\phi(x))}{\alpha!}(\nu)^\alpha.$$

All terms beyond these finite sums vanish because $\mathfrak J^{m+5}=0$; the rule for $K$ is the Taylor extension of a smooth real function in its $z,\bar z$ variables, and the rule for $W$ uses only its holomorphic Wirtinger derivatives.

For each $i=1,\ldots,n$, the full formal physical components are smooth maps $a^i,\mathcal F^i:M\to\mathcal G_{\bar0}$ and $\psi^i_\alpha:M\to\mathcal G_{\bar1}$, with compact support in spacetime $M$: equivalently each coefficient of each exterior-basis monomial is a compactly supported smooth complex function of $x$. Require the scalar body $\phi^i=b(a^i)$ to lie in $U$ jointly. The lowest chiral coefficient is $a^i$, not merely its body $\phi^i$; it may have even nilpotent terms. In the physical normalization definition instantiate its scalar and auxiliary component symbols by $a^i$ and $\mathcal F^i$, respectively:

$$\Phi^i(y,\theta)=a^i(y)+\sqrt2\theta^\alpha\psi^i_\alpha(y)+2\theta^1\theta^2\mathcal F^i(y),\qquad y=x+i\theta\sigma\bar\theta.$$

Barred component fields mean the specified coefficient involution, so $\bar a^{\bar i}=(a^i)^*$ and $\overline{\mathcal F}^{\bar i}=(\mathcal F^i)^*$; barred fermions are likewise the conjugates of the coefficient maps. On $\mathcal B$ use the supplier's graded-tensor involution, including $\theta^*=\bar\theta$ and reversal of all factors. The formal action has values in the even fixed real subspace of $\mathcal G$; no order or nonnegativity is assigned to nilpotent elements.

The supersymmetry parameters $\epsilon^\alpha,\bar\epsilon^{\dot\alpha}$ are constant odd coefficients, in $\mathcal G$ or a finite exterior extension equipped with the same involution. The adopted variation is $\delta\Phi^i=(\epsilon^\alpha Q_\alpha+\bar\epsilon^{\dot\alpha}\bar Q_{\dot\alpha})\Phi^i$ with the chiral-superfield supercharges. Formal parameter components may be treated independently for the algebraic identities; a conjugation-preserving variation in this left-parameter convention has $\bar\epsilon^{\dot\alpha}=-(\epsilon^\alpha)^*$ and $\delta\bar\Phi=(\delta\Phi)^*$. Indeed $\delta\theta=\epsilon$ and $\delta\bar\theta=-\bar\epsilon$ then commute with the chosen involution. The full even coefficient spaces for $a$ and $\mathcal F$ are retained under these transformations; the ordinary bosonic slice below need not be invariant. The engineering dimensions are $[x^\mu]=-1$, $[\theta]=[\bar\theta]=-1/2$, $[a^i]=1$, $[\psi^i]=3/2$, $[\mathcal F^i]=2$, $[K]=2$, and $[W]=3$ in mass units.

Adopt the classical action

$$S_{\mathrm{WZ}}=\int_M d^4x\left([K(\bar\Phi,\Phi)]_D+[W(\Phi)]_F+\mathrm{h.c.}\right),$$

Thus taking this sector commutes with the degree-zero augmentation, but it is a restriction for evaluating a bosonic action, not an assertion of off-shell supersymmetry closure on a purely complex field space. The component conversion below gives its complete bosonic Lagrangian, up to the displayed spacetime divergence,

$$\mathcal L_{\mathrm{bos}}=-g_{i\bar j}(\phi,\bar\phi)\eta^{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu\phi^i\partial_\nu\bar\phi^{\bar j}+g_{i\bar j}(\phi,\bar\phi)F^i\bar F^{\bar j}+F^iW_i(\phi)+\bar F^{\bar j}\overline{W_j(\phi)}+\tfrac14\Box K(\phi,\bar\phi),\qquad\Box=\eta^{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu\partial_\nu.$$

Its bosonic zero-derivative auxiliary terms are therefore precisely

$$\mathcal L_F=g_{i\bar j}(\phi,\bar\phi)F^i\bar F^{\bar j}+F^iW_i(\phi)+\bar F^{\bar j}\overline{W_j(\phi)}.$$

Only this ordinary complex sector is used for the ordered real scalar-potential and minimization conclusions. An arbitrary even $\mathcal G$-valued auxiliary field remains valid in the full formal model, but is not a vector in an ordered positive-definite complex metric space.

The canonical Wess–Zumino model is the special case $U=\mathbb C^n$, $K(z,\bar z)=\sum_i\bar z^{\bar i}z^i$, and hence $g_{i\bar j}=\delta_{i\bar j}$. This is an adopted classical formulation and normalization, not a deduction that nature realizes the model.

Equip it with the conjugate-linear, order-reversing involution $(\epsilon^\alpha)^*=-\bar\epsilon^{\dot\alpha}$ and $(\bar\epsilon^{\dot\alpha})^*=-\epsilon^\alpha$. The minus signs are the conjugation-compatible convention for parameters placed on the left: $\delta\theta^\alpha=\epsilon^\alpha$ and $\delta\bar\theta^{\dot\alpha}=-\bar\epsilon^{\dot\alpha}$ then respect $(\theta^\alpha)^*=\bar\theta^{\dot\alpha}$. The four generators remain independent over $\mathbb C$. Set $\mathcal A_\epsilon=\mathcal A\widehat\otimes\mathcal E$, where $\widehat\otimes$ denotes the graded tensor product: $(a\otimes u)(b\otimes v)=(-1)^{|u||b|}ab\otimes uv$ on homogeneous factors, with total parity and the order-reversing conjugation specified by the coefficient-algebra convention. This is again a finite-dimensional supercommutative coefficient algebra. Set $\mathscr S_\epsilon=C^\infty(\mathbb R^{1,3},\mathcal A_\epsilon\widehat\otimes\Lambda_4)$ and embed $\mathscr S$ into it by $a\mapsto a\otimes1$. The parameters commute with even elements and anticommute with odd elements of both $\mathcal A$ and $\Lambda_4$.

Extend the displayed coordinate derivatives to $\mathscr S_\epsilon$ by the same left-derivative rule, vanishing on $\mathcal A_\epsilon$; extend $Q_\alpha$ and $\bar Q_{\dot\alpha}$ by their displayed formulas. In particular, an odd derivative or supercharge acquires a minus sign when moved past an external odd parameter. Define the even complex-linear variation $\delta_{\epsilon,\bar\epsilon}:\mathscr S\to\mathscr S_\epsilon$ by

$$\delta_{\epsilon,\bar\epsilon}\Phi=\sum_\alpha\epsilon^\alpha Q_\alpha\Phi+\sum_{\dot\alpha}\bar\epsilon^{\dot\alpha}\bar Q_{\dot\alpha}\Phi.$$

For a chiral $\Phi$, the component transformation is the unique tuple $(\delta A,\delta\psi_1,\delta\psi_2,\delta F)$ of smooth $\mathcal A_\epsilon$-valued functions in the displayed $y,\theta$ expansion of $\delta_{\epsilon,\bar\epsilon}\Phi$, with $\delta A,\delta F$ even and $\delta\psi_\alpha$ odd. Chirality and uniqueness in this extended coefficient algebra are established by the local chiral-superspace identities. The same variation formula acts on $\mathscr S_\epsilon$ if repeated variations with these parameters are desired; adjoining further independent parameter copies uses the same graded tensor construction. The space of fields is classical and smooth: the coordinate differential operators act on all of $\mathscr S$, or all of $\mathscr S_\epsilon$ after scalar extension; no quantum-field operator domain or field equation is assumed. If $[\Phi]=d$ is assigned, the formal component dimensions are $[A]=d$, $[\psi_\alpha]=d+\tfrac12$, and $[F]=d+1$; no value of $d$ is fixed. The kernel of both $\bar D_{\dot\alpha}$ consists exactly of the fields independent of $\bar\theta$ when written in the nilpotently shifted coordinate $y^\mu=x^\mu+i\theta^\alpha\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\alpha}\bar\theta^{\dot\alpha}$; hence every chiral field has the unique four-component expansion stated there. The supercharges $Q_\alpha,\bar Q_{\dot\alpha}$ anticommute with each $\bar D_{\dot\beta}$, so the defined supersymmetry transformation preserves chirality and induces a unique smooth component transformation.

Let $\mathcal A=\mathcal A_{\bar0}\oplus\mathcal A_{\bar1}$ be a finite-dimensional $\mathbb Z_2$-graded complex algebra whose homogeneous elements satisfy $ab=(-1)^{|a||b|}ba$, equipped with a conjugate-linear parity-preserving involutive anti-automorphism $a\mapsto a^*$ extending complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$. For the ordered index set $J=\{1,2,3,4\}$, let $\Lambda_4$ be the complex vector space with specified basis $(e_S)_{S\subseteq J}$, including $e_\varnothing=1$. Define
$$ \nu(S,T)=|\{(s,t)\in S\times T:s>t\}|,\qquad e_Se_T=\begin{cases}0,&S\cap T\ne\varnothing,\\(-1)^{\nu(S,T)}e_{S\cup T},&S\cap T=\varnothing.\end{cases} $$
Put $\xi_1=\theta^1=e_{\{1\}}$, $\xi_2=\theta^2=e_{\{2\}}$, $\xi_3=\bar\theta^{\dot1}=e_{\{3\}}$, and $\xi_4=\bar\theta^{\dot2}=e_{\{4\}}$. Then each $\xi_i$ is odd, $\xi_i^2=0$, and $\xi_i\xi_j=-\xi_j\xi_i$ for $i\ne j$. Give $\Lambda_4$ the grading $|e_S|=|S|\bmod2$. The superspace coefficient vector space is $\mathcal A\otimes_\mathbb C\Lambda_4$ with total parity and graded-tensor multiplication
$$ (a\otimes e_S)(b\otimes e_T)=(-1)^{|S||b|}(ab)\otimes(e_Se_T) $$
for homogeneous $a,b$. On the basis, the left derivative removes $i$ with sign $(-1)^{|\{s\in S:s<i\}|}$ and the right derivative removes $i$ with sign $(-1)^{|\{s\in S:s>i\}|}$ when $i\in S$, and both give zero when $i\notin S$. On a coefficient-left homogeneous tensor $a\otimes e_S$, define $\partial^L_{\xi_i}(a\otimes e_S)=(-1)^{|a|}a\otimes\partial^L_{\xi_i}e_S$ and $\partial^R_{\xi_i}(a\otimes e_S)=a\otimes\partial^R_{\xi_i}e_S$; in particular both vanish on $a\otimes1$. The algebra axioms and derivative rules below are verified in the local well-definedness result. Complex conjugation on this coefficient algebra extends the given operation on $\mathcal A$ by $i^*=-i$, $(\theta^\alpha)^*=\bar\theta^{\dot\alpha}$, $(\bar\theta^{\dot\alpha})^*=\theta^\alpha$, and $(uv)^*=v^*u^*$. In the coefficient-left tensor notation this means $(a\otimes e_S)^*=(-1)^{|a||S|}a^*\otimes e_S^*$, where $e_S^*$ is obtained by reversing the ordered generator word for $e_S$ and applying the stated generator conjugation.

For each $i\in J$, the left derivative $\partial^L_{\xi_i}$ is the unique odd derivation of the graded tensor algebra that vanishes on $\mathcal A$ and has $\partial^L_{\xi_i}\xi_j=\delta_{ij}$; on homogeneous $u,v$ it obeys
$$ \partial^L_{\xi_i}(uv)=(\partial^L_{\xi_i}u)v+(-1)^{|u|}u(\partial^L_{\xi_i}v). $$
The right derivative $\partial^R_{\xi_i}$ is the unique right odd derivation vanishing on $\mathcal A$ with $\partial^R_{\xi_i}\xi_j=\delta_{ij}$ and
$$ \partial^R_{\xi_i}(uv)=(-1)^{|v|}(\partial^R_{\xi_i}u)v+u(\partial^R_{\xi_i}v). $$
For one generator, write a polynomial uniquely with that generator on the left as $f=f_0+\xi_i f_1$, with $f_0,f_1$ independent of $\xi_i$, and define its Berezin integral by the complex-linear coefficient-extraction rule $\int d\xi_i\,f=f_1$. Thus $\int d\xi_i\,1=0$ and $\int d\xi_i\,\xi_i=1$. Fix the ordered measures
$$ \int d^2\theta:=\int d\theta^2\,d\theta^1,\qquad \int d^2\bar\theta:=\int d\bar\theta^{\dot2}\,d\bar\theta^{\dot1},\qquad \int d^4\theta:=\int d\bar\theta^{\dot2}\,d\bar\theta^{\dot1}\,d\theta^2\,d\theta^1. $$
With this order, $\int d^4\theta$ extracts the coefficient of $\theta^1\theta^2\bar\theta^{\dot1}\bar\theta^{\dot2}$. For superspace coordinates $x=(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)\in\mathbb R^{1,3}$ in natural units $\hbar=c=1$, assign mass dimensions $[x^\mu]=-1$, $[\theta^\alpha]=[\bar\theta^{\dot\alpha}]=-\tfrac12$, $[d\theta^\alpha]=[d\bar\theta^{\dot\alpha}]=\tfrac12$, and hence $[d^2\theta]=[d^2\bar\theta]=1$ and $[d^4\theta]=2$. These are formal engineering dimensions; no physical model or empirical unit convention is asserted.

derivations.claim: For any even smooth superspace function $X$, substitute the operators from [F1] into $\delta X$. Since the odd parameters are constant, the odd Leibniz rule gives $\epsilon^\alpha\partial^L_{\theta^\alpha}X=-\partial^L_{\theta^\alpha}(\epsilon^\alpha X)$ and $-\bar\epsilon^{\dot\alpha}\partial^L_{\bar\theta^{\dot\alpha}}X=\partial^L_{\bar\theta^{\dot\alpha}}(\bar\epsilon^{\dot\alpha}X)$. The remaining terms are ordinary spacetime derivatives, so $\delta X=-\partial^L_{\theta^\alpha}(\epsilon^\alpha X)+\partial^L_{\bar\theta^{\dot\alpha}}(\bar\epsilon^{\dot\alpha}X)+\partial_\mu(-i\epsilon^\alpha\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\beta}\bar\theta^{\dot\beta}X+i\bar\epsilon^{\dot\alpha}\theta^\beta\sigma^\mu_{\beta\dot\alpha}X)$.

For a chiral superfield $X(y,\theta)$, use $y=x+i\theta\sigma\bar\theta$ and the left-derivative rules in [F1]–[F3]. The chain rule gives $Q_\alpha=\partial^L_{\theta^\alpha}|_y$ and $\bar Q_{\dot\alpha}=-\partial^L_{\bar\theta^{\dot\alpha}}|_y+2i\theta^\beta\sigma^\mu_{\beta\dot\alpha}\partial_{y^\mu}$. Since $X$ is independent of $\bar\theta$, $\delta X=\epsilon^\alpha\partial^L_{\theta^\alpha}X+2i\bar\epsilon^{\dot\alpha}\theta^\beta\sigma^\mu_{\beta\dot\alpha}\partial_\mu X$.

Expand the supercharge anticommutators from [F1]. The only nonzero terms in $\{Q_\alpha,\bar Q_{\dot\beta}\}$ are $\{\partial^L_{\theta^\alpha},i\theta^\gamma\sigma^\mu_{\gamma\dot\beta}\partial_\mu\}=i\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\beta}\partial_\mu$ and $\{-i\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\gamma}\bar\theta^{\dot\gamma}\partial_\mu,-\partial^L_{\bar\theta^{\dot\beta}}\}=i\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\beta}\partial_\mu$. Terms with two odd coordinates cancel under symmetrization, and derivatives in distinct generators anticommute by [F3]. Hence $\{Q_\alpha,\bar Q_{\dot\beta}\}=2i\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\beta}\partial_\mu$ and both same-chirality anticommutators are zero.

Apply step 1.1 to the even D-term integrand $X=K(\bar\Phi,\Phi)$, whose finite nilpotent Taylor expansion is smooth. Each odd-coordinate derivative has zero top coefficient in the ordered Grassmann basis from [F3], so its Berezin integral vanishes. The spacetime-divergence term integrates to zero because the field-dependent part of $K$ is compactly supported and its constant exterior value has zero supersymmetry variation. The fixed physical factor $-1/4$ multiplies zero, so the D-term action is invariant.

The first term in step 1.2 integrates to zero under $d^2\theta$ by the same coefficient-extraction calculation as step 2.1. The second is the spacetime divergence $\partial_\mu(2i\bar\epsilon^{\dot\alpha}\theta^\beta\sigma^\mu_{\beta\dot\alpha}X)$; compact support removes its boundary term. For the finite Taylor extension in the postulate, holomorphicity $\partial_{\bar i}W=0$ and the odd derivation rule give the chain identity $\bar D_{\dot\alpha}W(\Phi)=\sum_i W_i(\Phi)\bar D_{\dot\alpha}\Phi^i=0$, because each $\Phi^i$ is chiral; hence $W(\Phi)$ is chiral. Complex conjugation gives the corresponding antichirality of its conjugate. The fixed physical factor $1/2$ and its conjugate preserve this zero variation, so the F-term action is invariant.

Work in $\mathcal G_\epsilon$ for one variation, and adjoin a second independent exterior parameter copy for commutators of two variations. The operators extend by the graded derivative rule and annihilate the coefficient algebra, exactly as in [F1]. By [F2], the transformations preserve the chiral constraint, so the transformed field has the unique component expansion in [F1]. Coefficient extraction is linear; therefore the operator identities in step 1.3 induce the same translation algebra on every full formal component, including the independent even auxiliary coefficient $\mathcal F^i$. Products of odd parameters and odd component maps lie in the total even subspace $(\mathcal G_\epsilon)_{\bar0}$, while fermionic variations lie in its total odd subspace, and derivatives preserve coefficientwise compact support; thus this argument does not restrict the auxiliary coefficient to $\mathbb C$ or assert closure on the bosonic slice. No Euler–Lagrange equation was used, proving off-shell closure.

derivations.claim: Since $F^i$ occurs algebraically and without derivatives, its Euler–Lagrange equation is the ordinary partial derivative of $\mathcal L_F$ with respect to the independent conjugate coordinate $\bar F^{\bar j}$. Differentiating [A1] gives $g_{i\bar j}F^i+\bar W_{\bar j}=0$.

Therefore $\mathcal L_F$ equals this square minus $g^{\ell\bar k}W_\ell\bar W_{\bar k}$.
Positive definiteness makes $g$ invertible. Multiply the equation in step 1.1 by $g^{k\bar j}$ and use $g^{k\bar j}g_{i\bar j}=\delta_i^k$ to obtain $F^k=-g^{k\bar j}\bar W_{\bar j}$.

Substitute the solution from step 2.1: the square in step 1.2 vanishes, so the on-shell auxiliary Lagrangian is $-g^{i\bar j}W_i\bar W_{\bar j}$. To verify the sign directly, set $v^i=g^{i\bar j}\bar W_{\bar j}$. Hermitian symmetry and the inverse identities give $g^{i\bar j}W_i\bar W_{\bar j}=g_{i\bar j}v^i\bar v^{\bar j}$, which is positive when $v\ne0$ and zero when $v=0$. Thus the contraction is nonnegative; for $g_{i\bar j}=\delta_{i\bar j}$ it is $\sum_i|W_i|^2$. This is the classical scalar potential in the stated complex F-term sector; no order or positivity statement is made for general nilpotent coefficient-algebra values.
